sm: Paul Gigot, Joe Sternberg and Kate Bachelder Odell open by looking at what Congress can accomplish in its lame-duck session after a big Democratic election victory. They play the president's post-election interview on 60 Minutes, where he said his immigration crackdown both helped and hurt, and that deportation policy might have been too tough. The hosts say Trump has unique credibility with restrictionist Republicans to broker an immigration compromise, though they note that Stephen Miller, now chief of staff, favors keeping the issue alive. Sternberg says Republicans may be more willing to deal than Democrats, who may not want to sign anything with Trump. Nothing on immigration can happen before the next Congress.

The hosts turn to the near-term agenda. Trump endorsed a bipartisan Senate permitting compromise, while a former Biden climate adviser urged activists to kill it. They argue both parties have reasons to pass it, since renewable projects are also stuck in permitting, and that it would be an early test for Democrats on the economy. Other ideas include a defense package of about 350 billion dollars through reconciliation, indexing capital gains for inflation, welfare reforms and judicial confirmations. Odell notes that government funding expires on December 11th, and that Trump proposed a 1.5 trillion dollar defense budget, partly in reconciliation, while stopgap funding would keep the Pentagon near 840 billion dollars.

The hosts discuss defense funding further. They think Republicans should make any budget bill larger because this may be their last chance for a long time, but see little political courage for that. They expect Democrats to stick with current spending levels and demand large domestic spending in exchange for more defense money. Odell adds that Democrats want to bar funds for military operations against Iran, which could threaten the naval blockade. Gigot hopes at least for appellate judge confirmations. They then turn to Thomas Massie's motion to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which Hakeem Jeffries says he supports. Sternberg calls it a distraction that does not answer voters' real complaints about the Iran war.

The hosts argue that impeaching Hegseth is a gesture that will fail, since there are no votes to convict in the Senate, and that Trump will not fire him under pressure. Odell says the Iran outcome was the president's decision, though Hegseth is a polarizing figure. Sternberg says Democrats should focus on economic legislation such as permitting reform and limits on the president's tariff powers. Gigot says tariff repeal cannot pass in a Republican lame duck because Trump would veto it. Sternberg also suggests Democrats could press on Ukraine support, and says cutting off funding for the Iran blockade is the wrong lesson from the voters. Gigot closes by saying voters dislike excesses from both parties, as on immigration.
